How a plant keeps a growing pile of workflows under control: shared settings,
folders, annotated runs, redaction, numbers over time, outside secrets, log
streaming and where large data lives. Everything here is free and in every
build.

Every endpoint named below is in the OpenAPI document at
`/api/v1/openapi.json`, and every one has a test that calls it, on SQLite and on
Postgres.

## Variables

In the editor: Variables, in the top bar. Instance wide ones are at the top, and each project's under its name. Only what your role allows is offered.

A variable is a named value a workflow reads as `vars.NAME`: a setpoint ceiling,
a plant's name, a base URL that differs between the pilot line and the real one.

```yaml
- name: Check limit
  type: core.if
  version: 1
  params:
    condition: "{{ item.json.temp > toNumber(vars.TEMP_LIMIT) }}"
```

- A variable is **instance wide** or belongs to **one project**. Where both have
  a name, the project's wins, and only for that project's workflows.
- A value is text, up to 8 KiB. Use `toNumber(vars.X)` when you need a number.
- A name is letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter or an
  underscore, up to 64 long, because it has to read as `vars.NAME`.
- **Variables are not secrets.** Anyone who can read the project reads its
  variables, and the value is not scrubbed from run data. A password, a token or
  a key goes in the credential vault, or in an external secret store (below).
- A run reads its variables when it starts, and again if it resumes after a wait
  or a restart. A change reaches the next run, not one already in the middle of
  a step. A name that isn't there reads as nothing, not as an error.

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/v1/variables` | Instance variables and those in projects you can read; `?project=` narrows to one project. |
| `POST /api/v1/variables` | Make one. With `projectId` it's the project's, with none it's instance wide. |
| `PUT /api/v1/variables/{variable}` | Change its name and value. |
| `DELETE /api/v1/variables/{variable}` | Delete it. |

Who may: in a project, the `variable.read` permission lists them and
`variable.create`, `variable.update` and `variable.delete` change them. Viewers
and operators read, editors and admins change. Instance wide variables are
readable by anyone signed in, because any project's workflow can read them, and
only an instance owner or admin changes them. A custom role can carry any of
those four permissions. Changes are in the audit log as `variable.created`,
`variable.updated` and `variable.deleted`, with the name and never the value.

## Folders

In the editor: the workflow list is the folders. Make one with New folder, nest it with Add subfolder, and move a workflow from the list on its own row. Choosing a folder when you make a workflow puts it there.

Folders group a project's workflows and nest, the way a plant is laid out: area,
line, cell.

- A folder is in one project. Names are unique among the folders next to each
  other, and a name is up to 100 characters.
- Folders nest up to 10 deep.
- A workflow is in one folder or at the top of its project. Saving a new
  version doesn't move it.
- A folder with workflows or folders in it can't be deleted (409), so deleting a
  folder is never how a workflow goes missing. A folder can't be moved inside
  itself or one of its own subfolders, and can't be moved to another project.

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/v1/folders` | Folders in projects you can read, flat, each with its `parentId`; `?project=` narrows. |
| `POST /api/v1/folders` | Make one in `projectId`, inside `parentId` or at the top. |
| `PATCH /api/v1/folders/{folder}` | Rename it, or move it with `parentId` (empty string for the top). |
| `DELETE /api/v1/folders/{folder}` | Delete an empty folder. |
| `PUT /api/v1/workflows/{workflow}/folder` | Put a workflow in a folder, or at the top with an empty `folderId`. |
| `GET /api/v1/workflows?folder=` | One folder's workflows, or `folder=none` for the top of each project. |

Every workflow the API returns says its `folderId`. The `folder.read`,
`folder.create`, `folder.update` and `folder.delete` permissions work like the
variable ones, and moving a workflow takes `workflow.update`. Folder changes are
in the audit log, and moves as `workflow.moved`.

## Execution annotations

In the editor: every run's page has an Annotation box with a thumbs up or down, a note and tags, and the executions list filters by tag and by vote.

A person can say something about a run after it happened: a thumbs up or down, a
note, and tags to find it by. "First good batch after the die change" and
`scrap` are the kind of thing that goes here.

```sh
curl -X PUT $CASCADE/api/v1/executions/$RUN/annotation -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \
  -d '{"vote":"up","note":"first good batch after the die change","tags":["die-change","first-shift"]}'
```

- A vote is `up`, `down` or empty. A note is up to 2000 characters. A run has up
  to 20 tags, each 1 to 40 characters with no control characters, listed once.
- `PUT` replaces the whole annotation, so send everything you want kept. An
  annotation that says nothing is the same as none. `DELETE
  /api/v1/executions/{execution}/annotation` clears it.
- Every run the API returns carries its annotation, and the listing carries it
  on each row. `GET /api/v1/executions?tag=scrap` and `?vote=down` filter, and
  they combine with the other filters.
- The annotation records who left it and when, from the same identity the audit
  log uses.
- Annotating takes the `execution.annotate` permission, which operators,
  editors and admins have and viewers don't. Viewers read annotations.
- An annotation goes when its run is deleted. The audit log keeps
  `execution.annotated` and `execution.annotation_cleared` with the vote and
  tags, and records only that a note was left, not what it said.

## Execution redaction policies

In the editor: Settings, Redaction makes the policies. A workflow picks one in the editor's side panel with nothing selected, under Workflow settings.

The credential vault already keeps secrets out of everything a run stores. A
redaction policy is for the data that isn't a credential but doesn't belong in
the execution history either: a badge number, an operator's name, a card number
that came in on a webhook.

A policy is a name and rules:

- **fields**: item key names. A key a policy names has its whole value replaced
  with `[redacted]`, at any depth, whatever type the value is. Matching ignores
  case, and `*` and `?` work as wildcards, so `*secret*` takes `plant_secret`
  and `SecretKey`.
- **patterns**: regular expressions, in Go's RE2 syntax. Every match inside any
  text is replaced with `[redacted]`. A pattern that matches the empty text is
  refused.
- **steps**: optional. The policy covers only the steps listed. Empty means
  every step.
- **appliesToAll**: optional. The policy covers every workflow, whether or not
  it names the policy.

A workflow chooses one by name in its settings:

```yaml
settings:
  redaction: Badges
```

What it does and when:

- It runs **when the execution finishes**, in the same transaction that marks it
  finished: succeeded, failed or stopped. Until then the run has its real data,
  because the next step needs it and a restart resumes from it. A run that is
  waiting still holds its real data.
- It scrubs each step's stored output, each step's stored error message, the
  execution's own error, and a stored webhook answer. It doesn't touch file
  contents: a policy reads item data, and a file is a reference to bytes.
- What was stored is what a replay or a retry from the middle of that run will
  start from, so a replay sees the scrubbed values. The workflow's trigger items
  are in the first step's output, and they are scrubbed too.
- It reads the workflow as that run had it, so editing a workflow, or the
  policy, never changes a run that is already over.
- A workflow that names a policy that doesn't exist **fails closed**: its runs
  keep no item data at all, the way the `metadata` save setting works, and the
  workflow's `problems` say so. A missing policy must never mean data kept that
  somebody meant to scrub.
- A policy that workflows name can't be deleted (409), and its name can't change.
  Rules can.

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/v1/redaction-policies` | Every policy. Anyone signed in can read them, because the people who write workflows need the names. |
| `POST /api/v1/redaction-policies` | Make one. |
| `PUT /api/v1/redaction-policies/{policy}` | Replace its description and rules. |
| `DELETE /api/v1/redaction-policies/{policy}` | Delete one no workflow names. |

Making, changing and deleting a policy takes the instance `redaction.manage`
permission, which owners and admins have. Each is in the audit log as
`redaction.created`, `redaction.updated` and `redaction.deleted`.

## Insights

In the editor: Insights, in the top bar. Pick a window, a project and a workflow; it shows the totals, a chart and a table per day, and a table per workflow.

`GET /api/v1/insights` adds the runs in a window up: how they ended, how long
they took, per day and per workflow.

```sh
curl "$CASCADE/api/v1/insights?from=2026-10-10&to=2026-10-14&project=$PROJECT" -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY"
```

- `from` and `to` are an RFC 3339 time or a date (midnight UTC). With none, it's
  the last seven days up to now. The most it answers for is 366 days.
- `project` and `workflow` narrow it. Without them it counts every project the
  caller can read executions in, so each person's numbers are their own.
- A run counts on the UTC day it was created.
- `totals` and every row in `days` and `workflows` carry `total`, `succeeded`,
  `failed`, `canceled` and `unfinished` (queued, running or waiting), the
  average and longest run time in milliseconds over runs that have both a start
  and a finish, and `failureRate`.
- `failureRate` is failed over succeeded plus failed. A canceled run isn't a
  failure and an unfinished one hasn't decided, so neither is in it. It is 0
  when nothing has finished either way.
- `days` lists every UTC day in the window, with zeros for a day nothing ran, so
  a chart has no gaps to guess at. `workflows` is the 50 busiest, busiest first.

It reads the same execution rows the execution list does, so it needs the
`execution.read` permission and a key scoped for it.

## External secrets

In the editor: Settings, External secrets. Add a provider, try it against a path from the same card, and see what the reference for it looks like.

A credential's secret field can point at a secret kept in HashiCorp Vault or
OpenBao instead of holding the secret itself. Rotate the password in the store
and every workflow uses the new one on its next run, with nobody editing a
credential, and a copy of your database never holds the password.

A reference looks like this, in any secret field of a credential:

```
secret://bao/plant/line-3/db#password
```

That is the provider named `bao`, the secret at `plant/line-3/db`, and its
`password` key. The credential stores that text, sealed like any secret.
Nothing it points at is ever stored here: the value is read when a run opens
the credential, held in memory for the provider's cache time, and scrubbed from
everything the run saves, the same as a password in the vault. Only secret
fields take references. A reference typed into a field that isn't secret is just
text.

### Setting up a provider

A provider is the server, how Cascade signs in to it, and where it may read.
Making, changing and removing one is an instance owner or admin's, the
`secrets.manage` permission, and has to be done by a person signed in, not by an
API key.

```sh
curl -X POST $CASCADE/api/v1/secret-providers -H "X-CSRF-Token: ..." -d '{
  "name": "bao",
  "address": "https://bao.plant.example:8200",
  "authMethod": "approle", "roleId": "...", "secretId": "...",
  "allowedPaths": ["plant"]
}'
```

| Field | What it does |
|---|---|
| `name` | 1 to 40 lowercase letters, digits and dashes. It is in every reference, so it can't change later. |
| `address` | The server's URL. |
| `mount`, `kvVersion` | Where the KV engine is mounted (`secret` by default) and whether it is version 1 or 2 (2 by default). |
| `namespace` | Sent as `X-Vault-Namespace`, for a namespace of the server. |
| `authMethod` | `token` with `token`, or `approle` with `roleId` and `secretId`. `authMount` is where AppRole is mounted (`approle` by default). AppRole signs in itself and again when its token runs out. |
| `caCert` | A PEM certificate authority to trust for the server, when its certificate isn't from one the system trusts. |
| `allowedPaths` | **Required.** The only places a reference may read from. `plant` allows `plant` and everything under it, and not `plantation`. |
| `projects` | Optional. The only projects that may use the provider. Left empty, every project may. |
| `cacheSeconds` | How long a read secret is kept in memory, 0 to 3600. 30 by default. 0 reads every time. |

How Cascade signs in (the token, or the AppRole id and secret) is sealed under
the instance key, rewrapped by a key rotation with everything else, and never
shown by any call. Leave it out of a change and the stored one stays.

`POST /api/v1/secret-providers/{provider}/test` signs in and, with a `path`,
reads it, and says whether it worked. It never returns a value. `GET
/api/v1/secret-providers` lists providers for anyone signed in, because the
people who build credentials need the names. The calls are in the audit log as
`secrets.provider_created`, `_updated` and `_deleted`.

### What it won't do

- **A provider needs allowed paths.** A token for Vault can usually read far
  more than anyone who edits credentials should be able to name, and without a
  list, anyone who can make a credential could point one at any secret the token
  can reach and have a workflow send it somewhere. Give the provider the paths
  its credentials need and its policy the same.
- **A reference is checked when the credential is saved**, not only when a run
  uses it: the provider has to exist, be open to the credential's project, and
  allow the path. A path with an empty part, a dot, or a `..` is refused.
- **A run that can't read the secret fails and says why**, naming the provider,
  the path and the key and never a value: no such provider, a path the
  provider doesn't allow, no secret there, no such key, or the server's own
  refusal (a policy that doesn't allow the read is "permission denied").
- **Deleting a provider doesn't edit credentials.** Ones that point at it fail
  when a run opens them, saying the provider is gone.
- A secret value that really begins with `secret://` can't be stored as a
  secret, because it reads as a reference.
- Values that are numbers or true or false are read as text. A value that is a
  whole object or a list is refused.
## Log streaming

In the editor: Settings, Log streaming (owners and admins). Each destination shows how much it has sent, when it last delivered and its last error, with a button that sends one test event.

Send the audit log, and a line for every run that finishes, to the places a
plant already keeps its logs: a syslog server, or anything that takes OTLP logs
over HTTP (an OpenTelemetry collector, Loki, a log platform). Events leave as
they happen, so a SIEM sees a failed sign-in in seconds, and the audit trail
exists somewhere an administrator of this instance can't rewrite.

A destination is one place. Make as many as you need:

```sh
curl -X POST $CASCADE/api/v1/log-destinations -H "X-CSRF-Token: ..." -d '{
  "name": "plant syslog", "kind": "syslog",
  "address": "syslog.plant.example:6514", "network": "tls",
  "caCert": "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----..."
}'
curl -X POST $CASCADE/api/v1/log-destinations -H "X-CSRF-Token: ..." -d '{
  "name": "collector", "kind": "otlp", "endpoint": "https://otel.plant.example/v1/logs",
  "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer ..."}
}'
```

Making, changing and removing destinations is for instance owners and admins
(`logstream.manage`), by a person signed in and not by an API key, because a
destination is where the audit log goes. The calls are in the audit log as
`logstream.destination_created`, `_updated` and `_deleted`.

### What is sent

- **Audit events**: every row of the audit log, with its sequence number and its
  hash. The sequence number and the hash are how a receiver spots a repeat, and
  the hash is the row's own, so the chain can be checked from what arrived. A
  failed or refused sign-in is a warning, everything else a notice.
- **Execution events**: one for each run that finishes, whatever way it ends:
  the run's id, the workflow's id and name, its project, status, mode, when it
  was created, started and finished, how long it ran, and its error and the step
  it failed at. A failed run is an error, a stopped one a notice, a good one
  informational. They are sent a couple of seconds after the run ends.
- **Never item data.** What a run's steps saw and made stays in the run, where
  redaction policies protect it. The audit log never holds a secret.

`events` picks one or both (`["audit"]`, `["execution"]`, the default both).
`start` says where a new destination begins: `now`, the default, sends what
happens after it is made, and `beginning` sends the whole audit log and every
finished run first.

### Syslog

A message is RFC 5424: `<priority>1 time host hotloop-cascade pid msgid - {json}`,
with the event as one line of JSON. The priority is the facility times eight plus
the severity. The msgid is the audit action (`workflow.saved`) or the run's
status.

| Field | What it does |
|---|---|
| `address` | `host:port`. |
| `network` | `tcp` (the default), `udp` or `tls`. |
| `framing` | For `tcp` and `tls`: `octet` (RFC 6587 octet counting, the default) or `newline`. UDP is one datagram each. |
| `facility` | `local0` by default; any syslog facility name. |
| `appName` | The header's APP-NAME, `hotloop-cascade` by default. |
| `caCert`, `serverName` | For `tls`: the authority to trust, and the name the certificate has to be for when it isn't the host. There is no setting that skips the check. |

### OTLP

Logs go to `endpoint` as OTLP over HTTP with a JSON body: a log record for each
event, its body the event as JSON, and its parts as attributes
(`cascade.event`, `cascade.action`, `cascade.status`, `cascade.project`,
`cascade.actor.name` and so on) so a receiver can filter without parsing. The
resource says `service.name=hotloop-cascade`, its version and the host.
`headers` are sent with every request, for a token or a tenant. They are sealed
under the instance key, rewrapped by a key rotation, and never shown: the list
says only their names. `caCert` and `serverName` work as for syslog.

### How delivery behaves

- **At least once, in order.** A destination remembers the last audit row and
  the last finished run it sent. One that is down gets everything it missed when
  it comes back, in order, and a restart carries on where it stopped. If the
  sender is cut off between sending and noting it, those events are sent again,
  which is what the sequence numbers are for.
- **A failing destination backs off**, one second and doubling to five minutes,
  and its status says what went wrong and when: `lastError`, `lastErrorAt`. A
  success clears it. Nothing is dropped while it is down, so the audit log is the
  limit, not a queue.
- **One sender at a time.** With several mains, whichever holds a destination's
  lease sends to it; the others wait and take over if it stops.
- **Changing a destination keeps its place.** Moving it to another address never
  resends or skips anything. Headers left out of a change are kept, and an empty
  object clears them. The name and kind can't change.
- `POST /api/v1/log-destinations/{destination}/test` sends one made-up event
  through the same path and says whether it arrived, with the reason when it
  didn't. It moves nothing.
- `GET /api/v1/log-destinations` shows each one's status: how many events it has
  sent, the last audit sequence number delivered, when it last succeeded, and its
  last error.

## Where large data lives

Files and big payloads that a run carries (a downloaded PDF, a camera frame, a
spreadsheet) are stored as blobs, apart from the database. By default they sit
on the instance's disk. Set `HOTLOOP_CASCADE_BLOB_STORE` to put them in an S3
bucket or an Azure blob container instead, so the main can be rebuilt without
carrying them and several mains share one copy.

| Setting | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `HOTLOOP_CASCADE_BLOB_STORE` | `fs` (the default), `s3`, or `azure`. |
| `HOTLOOP_CASCADE_BLOB_SPOOL_DIR` | Where a blob waits while it is hashed before upload. Defaults to `blob-spool` in the data directory. |
| `HOTLOOP_CASCADE_BLOB_S3_BUCKET`, `_ACCESS_KEY`, `_SECRET_KEY` | Required for `s3`. The secret also reads `_SECRET_KEY_FILE`. |
| `HOTLOOP_CASCADE_BLOB_S3_ENDPOINT`, `_REGION` | Leave the endpoint out for AWS. Set it for Garage, MinIO or Ceph. |
| `HOTLOOP_CASCADE_BLOB_S3_PATH_STYLE` | `true` or `false`. Path style is the default whenever an endpoint is set. |
| `HOTLOOP_CASCADE_BLOB_S3_CA_FILE` | A CA bundle for an endpoint with a private certificate. |
| `HOTLOOP_CASCADE_BLOB_S3_PREFIX` | A folder inside the bucket, so one bucket can hold more than one instance. |
| `HOTLOOP_CASCADE_BLOB_AZURE_CONTAINER` | Required for `azure`. |
| `HOTLOOP_CASCADE_BLOB_AZURE_CONNECTION_STRING`, or `_ACCOUNT` with `_KEY`, or `_SAS` | One way to sign in. Secrets also read a `_FILE` form. |
| `HOTLOOP_CASCADE_BLOB_AZURE_ENDPOINT`, `_PREFIX` | An endpoint for Azurite or a private cloud, and a folder inside the container. |

On the chart, set these through `env` and `extraEnv`, with the secrets coming from
a Kubernetes Secret.

- **Addressed by content.** A blob is stored under its SHA-256 (`sha256/ab/cdef...`),
  so the same file is stored once however many runs carry it. Putting it again is
  a no-op, including when two runs do it at the same moment.
- **Hashed before upload.** The data is read once into the spool file, hashed,
  and then sent, so memory stays flat for any size. A blob over the size limit is
  refused, and a cancelled upload leaves nothing behind in the bucket.
- **Checked on the way out.** A read is verified against its hash as it streams,
  so a corrupted object fails loudly instead of handing a run bad data.
- **Size.** A single upload goes up as a multipart transfer on S3 and in blocks on
  Azure, so the usual 5 GiB single-request limit does not apply.
- **Changing store later.** Existing blobs stay where they were written. Move
  them to the new store before switching, because a reference to a blob the new
  store lacks is a missing file.

These two backends are tried against Garage and Azurite in the test stack, the
same conformance suite as the disk store: put and read, empty blobs, dedupe under
concurrency, corruption, the limit, bad ids, delete, list, a cancelled put, and a
192 MiB streamed upload with a heap check.

What it means for you: a rebuilt or replaced main finds every file its runs
carried, with no copying.
